strengths: The conceptual idea of leveraging affordance-aware textual descriptions (such as grasp taxonomy, object shape, and intent) inferred by vision-language models to resolve occlusion ambiguities in 3D hand reconstruction is intuitive and interesting.
The qualitative results demonstrate reasonable pose completions for heavily occluded fingers where standard regression baselines like HaMeR produce inaccurate configurations.
Under high occlusion, the diffusion-based refinement exhibits a noticeable reduction in PA-MPJPE (from 21.3 mm to 16.4 mm) on the evaluated subset.
weaknesses: Reliance on ground-truth grasp annotations: In Section 2.1 (Step 2), the authors state that because classifying grasp taxonomy with VLMs is difficult, they 'rely on the ground truth annotations provided by HOGraspNet to supply accurate taxonomy information for our framework.' This turns the pipeline into an oracle-assisted setup rather than an autonomous reconstruction method, making the comparison against baselines like HaMeR unfair.

Extremely limited quantitative evaluation: The experimental validation is conducted on only 300 instances sub-sampled from a single dataset (HOGraspNet). There are no experiments on standard, widely used hand-object interaction benchmarks such as DexYCB, HO3D, or OakInk.

Marginal overall improvement: The overall average PA-MPJPE only improves by 0.23 mm over HaMeR (from 8.51 mm to 8.28 mm), which suggests that the refinement has minimal impact on the vast majority of standard scenarios and may risk introducing artifacts when occlusion is low.

Lack of essential ablation studies: The paper lacks component-wise ablations evaluating the importance of each attribute in the affordance prompt (e.g., object size vs. shape vs. grasp taxonomy), nor does it evaluate performance when grasp taxonomy is predicted by a model rather than taken from ground truth.

Missing technical details: The manuscript is exceptionally short (only 4 pages of main text) and lacks crucial implementation details, such as the exact mathematical formulation and loss function for the 2D keypoint fitting during reverse diffusion, training hyperparameters, inference runtime, and network capacity.

strengths: The conceptual motivation is intuitive and sound: using rich textual affordance descriptions (e.g., grasp taxonomy, object attributes, and interaction intent) to guide generative priors for resolving hand pose ambiguities under severe occlusion.

The proposed modular framework is clearly presented, combining vision-language parsing, LLM summarization, occlusion mask reasoning (via ray casting and SAM2), and diffusion-based pose refinement conditioned on text.
Quantitative results in Table 1 demonstrate promising error reduction specifically under heavy occlusion (dropping from 21.3 mm to 16.4 mm PA-MPJPE on the high-occlusion subset).
weaknesses: Severe test-time information leak / reliance on ground truth: In Section 2.1, the authors explicitly state: 'We find that classifying grasp taxonomy with existing vision-language models is highly challenging. Consequently, we rely on the ground truth annotations provided by HOGraspNet [3] to supply accurate taxonomy information for our framework.' Using ground-truth grasp taxonomy labels at test time confers an unfair advantage over baseline vision-only estimators like HaMeR and undermines the claim of single-image 3D hand reconstruction.

Extremely limited evaluation scale: Quantitative evaluation is conducted on only 300 sampled test instances from a single dataset (HOGraspNet). Standard hand-object benchmarks (e.g., HO3D, DexYCB, OakInk) are entirely missing.

Lack of essential ablation studies: The submission contains no component ablations. It is unclear how much of the performance gain stems purely from the ground-truth grasp taxonomy versus the VLM-predicted object attributes (size, shape, interaction). Additionally, the components for occlusion reasoning (SAM2 mask + ray casting) and diffusion noise scheduling are unvalidated.

Incomplete submission length and depth: The manuscript contains only 4 pages of main text and is missing detailed mathematical descriptions (e.g., the exact formulation of the 2D keypoint fitting objective during reverse diffusion), broader baseline comparisons, runtime/computational overhead analysis, and discussion of failure modes. It is not ready for publication as a full conference paper.

strengths: Leveraging functional affordance and grasp taxonomy descriptions as a contextual prior to resolve severe hand-object occlusions is a conceptually interesting direction.
The proposed framework introduces a structured two-stage prompting approach (parsing interaction elements with a VLM and summarizing with an LLM) to construct affordance conditioning.
The method demonstrates notable error reductions under the high-occlusion subset (11+ occluded joints) on HOGraspNet.
weaknesses: Unfair reliance on ground-truth annotations at test time: In Section 2.1, the authors explicitly state: 'We find that classifying grasp taxonomy with existing vision-language models is highly challenging. Consequently, we rely on the ground truth annotations provided by HOGraspNet [3] to supply accurate taxonomy information for our framework.' Using ground-truth grasp labels at inference time gives the method an oracle advantage and invalidates fair benchmarking against methods like HaMeR.

Extremely limited and statistically weak evaluation: Quantitative experiments are conducted on only 300 sampled instances from a single dataset (HOGraspNet). For a full conference submission, evaluation should be comprehensive across full test splits and standard hand-object interaction benchmarks (e.g., DexYCB, OakInk, HO3D). Furthermore, the overall improvement across all cases is marginal (8.51 mm to 8.28 mm, a 0.23 mm difference).

Incomplete submission and missing technical depth: At only 4 pages of main text, the manuscript lacks essential sections and details. The mathematical formulation of the refinement process and 2D keypoint fitting during reverse diffusion is completely omitted, merely referencing prior work without specifying guidance functions, loss terms, or projection formulations.

Excessive pipeline complexity and unaddressed computational cost: The inference framework chains multiple heavy models together (Qwen2.5-VL, Mistral-7B, SAM2, CLIP, HaMeR, and a multi-step diffusion model). There is no analysis of runtime, computational efficiency, latency, or robustness against compounding errors/hallucinations from the vision-language models.
